items.question: A national grid operator is replacing a fifteen-year-old rules engine that assigns a hazard category to field work orders. A misclassification that downgrades a hazard sends a crew out without gas-detection equipment, which the safety team logs as a reportable incident. Offline evaluation on 4,000 historical work orders shows the Claude-based classifier agrees with the rules engine on 96% of them; on the 160 disagreements, a safety expert judged the classifier correct in 71 cases. Vendor support for the rules engine ends in eight weeks, and the safety team will not make the classifier authoritative without evidence it does not downgrade hazards on live work. Which rollout approach fits?

options.A: Cut over on the support deadline and keep the rules engine deployed as a fallback that operations can re-enable within one shift if reportable incidents rise above the current baseline.
options.B: Restrict the classifier to the lowest hazard category first and expand one category at a time, limiting the blast radius of any single misclassification during the early weeks.
options.C: Run both systems on live work orders with the rules engine still authoritative, route every disagreement to a safety reviewer, and cut over once the disagreement log shows the classifier is not the side downgrading hazards.
options.D: Expand the offline evaluation to 20,000 historical work orders and gate cutover on reaching 99% agreement with the rules engine, giving a much tighter confidence interval than 4,000 cases.

items.question: An online grocer ships a Claude-powered substitution suggester inside its picker mobile app. Prompts live in the application repository as string constants and ship with the binary; the mobile release train runs fortnightly and app-store review adds a further two to four days. A prompt change last month caused allergen-conflicting substitutions to be suggested, and the corrected prompt took nine days to reach pickers. The postmortem action item is titled "reduce time-to-remediate for prompt-caused defects". Which change addresses that action item most directly?

options.A: Add a regression evaluation suite to continuous integration that blocks the merge of any prompt change failing the allergen test cases before it can reach the release train.
options.B: Move to a weekly release train and pre-stage signed builds so app-store review overlaps with the internal QA window rather than following it.
options.C: Add a server-side output filter that drops any suggested substitution conflicting with allergens declared on the customer's account before it is shown to the picker.
options.D: Serve prompts from a versioned server-side configuration store the app fetches at session start, so a prompt version can be reverted without an app release.

items.question: A telco is transferring a Claude-based tier-one support deflection bot to a 24/7 network operations centre that has never operated an AI system. The NOC's entire alert catalogue is availability- and latency-based. The failure the product team fears is that the bot returns a fluent, confidently wrong answer while every endpoint is healthy and every latency objective is green. Which additions to the NOC's alert catalogue address that specific failure mode? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: An alert on p99 model-call latency, since degraded answer quality reliably shows up first as slower generation.
options.B: A rolling alert on the proportion of conversations that end in escalation to a human agent, compared against the same weekday in the previous week.
options.C: An alert on daily token spend deviating from the thirty-day trend by more than the agreed tolerance.
options.D: An alert on the rate at which answers fail the citation checker that grounds each claim in a knowledge-base article.
options.E: An alert on 5xx rates from the model gateway, paging the on-call engineer as soon as the error budget for the hour has been exhausted rather than at the end of the day.

items.question: A logistics company is handing a Claude-based customs-document extraction service to a managed-services vendor that will own L1 and L2 response under a 24/7 contract. The vendor's engineers have no context on the system and will act on the runbook alone at three in the morning. Which items belong in that runbook? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The architecture decision record explaining why customs extraction was implemented as a fixed workflow rather than an autonomous agent, with the options rejected.
options.B: The exact procedure to revert to the previously pinned prompt and model versions, including the command, the flag, and whose approval is required.
options.C: A catalogue of failure signatures already seen in production, each with its observable symptom and the first diagnostic query to run against the trace store.
options.D: The full evaluation set and grading rubric used to gate releases, so the vendor can re-run evaluation overnight and approve a fix before it ships to production.
options.E: The escalation path with named owners and the explicit conditions that require waking the product team rather than the vendor continuing to work the incident.

items.question: Two weeks before go-live for a Claude-based prior-authorisation summariser at a regional health plan, the production readiness review returns green on every item except one: there is no agreed procedure for what clinicians do when the summariser is unavailable or when a guardrail withholds its output. Volume is 3,000 authorisations a day and the fully manual path takes a nurse about twelve minutes per case. What is the next step?

options.A: Define and rehearse the degraded-mode procedure, including which cases queue and which are triaged manually, and hold go-live until clinical operations signs it off.
options.B: Go live on schedule and add the degraded-mode procedure to the first post-launch iteration, since every other readiness item is green and the expected outage rate is low.
options.C: Add an automatic fallback to a cheaper model tier so a summary is always produced, which removes the need for a manual procedure entirely.
options.D: Fund enough additional nursing capacity to absorb the six hundred nurse-hours a day that a total outage of the summariser would create.

items.question: In a ring-based phased rollout of a production AI feature, what should determine when the next ring opens?

options.A: A fixed calendar interval fixed in the release plan and communicated to stakeholders in advance.
options.B: Pre-declared exit criteria evaluated against the current ring's own production traffic.
options.C: Completion of user training and enablement for the population in the next ring.
options.D: The point at which support ticket volume from the current ring falls back to its pre-launch level.

items.question: A legal-tech vendor sells a contract-clause extraction API to sixty law firms. Its service pins one Claude model version, and its customer contracts promise that extraction behaviour will not change without ninety days' notice. The pinned version has entered its deprecation window, with retirement eleven months away. Six customers run their own downstream regression suites keyed to exact output strings. What should the vendor do first?

options.A: Introduce a versioned API surface, keeping v1 on the current behaviour and offering v2 on the successor model, and let each firm migrate on its own schedule.
options.B: Send the ninety-day notice to all sixty firms immediately, since the contractual clock should start as early as possible and the underlying model is definitely changing at some point in the next eleven months.
options.C: Run the successor model in shadow against production traffic, diff the outputs per customer, and use the diff to determine who is materially affected and what the notice must actually say.
options.D: Insert an output-normalisation layer that rewrites the successor's output into the current model's formatting so that no customer observes a change at all.

items.question: A manufacturer replaced a two-hundred-rule expert system for warranty-claim eligibility with a Claude-based decisioner six months ago. The old engine still runs in parallel at £14,000 a month in licence and hosting, and nobody has decommissioned it. Pressed by the finance director, the team's honest answer is that three of the two hundred rules encode a regulatory carve-out that nobody has verified in the new system. What is the correct sunset action?

options.A: Decommission now and add a post-hoc filter for the carve-out later if a claim is ever found to have been handled incorrectly under it.
options.B: Keep the old engine running permanently as the authoritative check on carve-out cases, treating the licence cost as the price of demonstrable compliance.
options.C: Port all two hundred rules verbatim into the decisioner's system prompt so behaviour is provably equivalent, then decommission the engine.
options.D: Write evaluations that exercise the three carve-out rules specifically, confirm the decisioner honours them, add those evaluations to the regression suite, and decommission on a dated plan.

items.question: A claims-processing centre deployed a Claude-based first-pass claim summariser. Staff were told headcount will not be cut but that per-handler throughput targets rise from thirty to forty-five claims a day on the day the tool launched. Adoption in week three is 19%. Interviews find handlers do not trust the summaries and are re-reading the full claim file anyway, which makes them slower than before. Which two actions most directly address the cause the interviews revealed? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Publish per-handler adoption leaderboards to the floor so peer comparison drives usage up.
options.B: Move the summariser to a higher-capability model tier to raise summary quality before pushing adoption further.
options.C: Suspend the throughput target increase until measured handling time with the tool is at or below the pre-tool baseline.
options.D: Mandate use of the tool through a policy signed by the operations director and audit compliance weekly.
options.E: Make the summariser cite the exact page and paragraph behind every factual assertion, so a handler can verify a point in seconds instead of re-reading the file.

items.question: At a bank, the trade-surveillance team reviews Claude-generated alert narratives before they are filed. In the pilot, reviewers approved 94% of narratives; a blind audit of the approved set found 8% contained a material factual error. Training to date has covered how to operate the tool. Which additions to the enablement programme address the pattern the audit revealed? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A module on transformer architecture and sampling so reviewers understand the mechanism that produces factual errors in generated narratives.
options.B: Calibration sessions on batches containing seeded incorrect narratives, with each reviewer scored on detection and debriefed afterwards.
options.C: A quick-reference card of prompt patterns reviewers can use to regenerate any narrative they feel unsure about before approving it.
options.D: A minimum four-minute dwell time per narrative, enforced in the tool before the approve control becomes active.
options.E: Ongoing blind re-audit of a sample of approved narratives, with results fed back to the individual reviewer who approved them.

items.question: A media company launched a Claude-based subtitle-localisation QA assistant. Leadership has proposed a quarterly steering review as the only post-launch checkpoint. The team ships prompt changes weekly and the content mix shifts seasonally. During the pilot, quality dipped and the team could not tell which of the eleven prompt changes made since the previous look had caused it. What review cadence should the architect argue for?

options.A: Quarterly steering only, backed by automated alerting on quality thresholds so that humans get involved exactly when a threshold is breached rather than on a fixed schedule that may find nothing.
options.B: A single monthly review at all levels, replacing both the weekly operational rhythm and the quarterly steering meeting with one consistent cadence.
options.C: A weekly operational review of quality metrics and sampled failures owned by the delivery team, with the quarterly steering review retained for scope and budget.
options.D: A review triggered by each prompt change rather than at fixed intervals, so every change is examined at the moment it ships.

items.question: Three months after launch, a travel company's Claude-based itinerary-change assistant has a crowded improvement backlog. Production data: hallucinated fare rules appear in 0.6% of the 40,000 conversations a month, and each one that reaches a customer costs £180 on average in goodwill refunds; tone is criticised in 22% of CSAT free-text comments; p95 latency is 4.1 seconds against a 3-second internal target; and a requested Portuguese expansion would open a market worth £2m a year in bookings at a 4% margin. Which should be prioritised first?

options.A: Bring p95 latency under the three-second target, since it is the only stated service objective currently in breach and breaches tend to compound as volume grows.
options.B: Ship the Portuguese expansion while the market opportunity is uncontested, deferring quality work to the following quarter when the revenue can fund it.
options.C: Address the tone complaints, which affect the largest share of customers who took the trouble to comment and shape the brand impression the assistant creates.
options.D: Cut the fare-rule hallucination rate, and gate other changes behind a groundedness evaluation until it comes down.

items.question: A build team is transferring a production Claude system to a separate run team. Which condition most reliably indicates the transfer is genuinely complete?

options.A: The run team has independently executed a rollback and a pinned-model-version change in production, unaided, with the build team absent.
options.B: The run team has attended an architecture walkthrough and received the full handover documentation pack.
options.C: The build team has closed every open defect on the backlog and the change freeze has been lifted.
options.D: Dashboards and alert routing have been repointed to the run team's on-call rota and paging schedule.

items.question: When an AI system is replacing an incumbent production system, what is the purpose of a parallel run?

options.A: To split load across both systems during transition so neither has to be provisioned for full production capacity.
options.B: To record where the two systems disagree on live traffic while the incumbent stays authoritative.
options.C: To let each user choose which system to work in, making adoption voluntary and reducing resistance to the change.
options.D: To satisfy a control requiring that two independent systems approve every transaction on an ongoing basis.

items.question: A pharmacy chain is designing a pilot for a Claude-based prescription-interaction checker. Two designs cost the same: six pharmacies for twelve weeks, or sixty pharmacies for two weeks. Each pharmacy dispenses roughly 400 scripts a week. The failure the safety board cares about is a missed interaction involving a drug that appears in fewer than one in five thousand scripts. Which design should the architect recommend?

options.A: Six pharmacies for twelve weeks, because a longer exposure lets pharmacists' override behaviour stabilise past the novelty period and gives a truer picture of steady-state use.
options.B: Sixty pharmacies for two weeks, because it puts roughly 48,000 scripts through the checker against 28,800 for the alternative, so more of the rare interactions actually occur.
options.C: Either duration, provided the rare-interaction failure is tested offline on a constructed set of known interaction cases and the pilot is used for what only live use reveals: workflow fit and override behaviour.
options.D: Neither yet; postpone the pilot until offline agreement with the chain's existing interaction database exceeds 99.9%, since safety work should not begin in live pharmacies at all.

items.question: A B2B SaaS company finished a four-week pilot of a Claude-based onboarding-email drafter. The criterion agreed before the pilot was: median time to send a first onboarding email drops from 22 minutes to under 10, with no increase in the 30-day churn rate of accounts onboarded during the pilot. Median time came in at 8 minutes. The churn figure cannot exist for another 30 days because the pilot cohort has only just onboarded. The sponsor wants a go/no-go today. What is the next step?

options.A: Declare a no-go, because a criterion that cannot be evaluated at the decision point must be treated as unmet.
options.B: Declare a go on the strength of the time result, since churn is a lagging indicator that would not have been available in time for any four-week pilot's decision.
options.C: Agree a leading proxy for churn, such as seven-day activation rate on the pilot cohort, and read the go/no-go against that proxy instead.
options.D: Hold the decision for 30 days with the pilot cohort still running, and tell the sponsor the churn half of the criterion is why the decision waits.

items.question: A rail operator wants a Claude-based depot assistant with three capabilities: answering engineers' questions from maintenance manuals, drafting fault reports, and automatically raising parts orders in the ERP. Funding covers one phase before the board's next review in sixteen weeks, and the board will decide continued funding on demonstrated value. The ERP write path needs a security review that the security team estimates at ten to fourteen weeks and cannot begin for another six. Fault-report drafting reuses the manuals index already built for question answering and needs no new integration. What should phase one contain?

options.A: Question answering over the manuals only, read-only, deferring everything else so the first phase carries the smallest possible surface area into the board review.
options.B: Question answering plus fault-report drafting, both read-only, with the engineer submitting the report.
options.C: All three capabilities behind a feature flag, with the ERP write path built and shipped disabled so it can be switched on the day the security review clears.
options.D: Parts ordering first, since it carries the largest quantified saving, running the security review in parallel with development so the two complete together.

items.question: What must a production readiness review for a Claude-based feature cover that a conventional service readiness review typically does not?

options.A: Capacity planning and load testing against projected peak throughput with agreed headroom.
options.B: A rollback path for the prompt and pinned model version, and alerting on output quality rather than availability alone.
options.C: An on-call rotation with paging thresholds and agreed incident severity definitions.
options.D: Backup and restore procedures for the feature's persistent state, tested end to end against the agreed recovery time objective.

items.question: A manufacturer's run team has inherited a Claude-based supplier-email triage service. The team's existing severity matrix defines S1 as service unavailable, S2 as degraded latency, and S3 as cosmetic. In the first month a prompt change broke two routing categories and roughly 300 supplier emails went to the wrong queue over four days. No incident was ever raised, because the service was up and inside its latency objective the whole time. What should the run team change?

options.A: Require the product team to review and approve every prompt change before it can be promoted to production.
options.B: Produce a daily routing report that a run-team engineer samples by hand each morning to spot anomalies.
options.C: Add severity definitions keyed to output-correctness thresholds, so a sustained misroute rate is an S1 or S2 regardless of availability.
options.D: Move the triage service to a higher-capability model tier so that routing mistakes of this kind become substantially less likely, and re-run the routing evaluation afterwards to confirm the improvement.

items.question: A regional bank is rolling out a Claude-based mortgage-document checker to 140 underwriters. The programme director's communications plan consists of a launch email and a recorded demo. HR has separately told the works council that no roles will be cut, with no timeframe attached. Underwriters have heard that a sister division introduced a similar tool shortly before a restructure. The bank's internal survey shows staff rate their line manager as the most trusted source of information about change and programme-team email as the least. Which two additions to the plan address the risk the survey and the rumour together describe? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: An expanded demo recording covering advanced features and prompt technique, so that underwriters get more out of the tool once they begin using it in earnest.
options.B: An anonymous feedback form so underwriters can raise concerns without attaching their names to them.
options.C: Line-manager briefings that address the job-security question head-on, sourced from the commitment HR has already given the works council.
options.D: A named network of underwriter peers who use the tool first and answer questions inside their own teams.
options.E: A written commitment from the chief executive that no underwriting roles will be cut for twenty-four months.

items.question: Why should a production AI release record bind the prompt version, the pinned model version and the gating evaluation run together under one identifier?

options.A: So that any behaviour change observed in production can be attributed to a specific, reproducible configuration.
options.B: Because model providers require the full configuration to be declared before a support request can be opened.
options.C: Because prompt registries can hold only one active version per environment, so binding the components together is what allows more than one configuration to be staged at a time.
options.D: Because evaluation results expire and must be re-run at deployment time to remain valid.

items.question: A SaaS HR platform plans to retire a Claude-based candidate-CV summarisation feature. Telemetry shows 4% of tenants use it at all, but two enterprise tenants generate 61% of its calls, and both are in renewal negotiation this quarter. Product wants to announce end-of-life in the next release note. What should happen first?

options.A: Publish the release note as planned; only 4% of tenants use the feature, and a single broad announcement treats every customer identically and fairly.
options.B: Keep the feature alive indefinitely behind a legacy flag for the two heavy tenants and remove it from the product for everyone else.
options.C: Swap the feature for a general-purpose summarisation endpoint without announcing anything, so no tenant has to act on a deprecation notice.
options.D: Contact the two tenants directly with a migration path and a dated timeline before any general announcement goes out.

items.question: A tax agency is migrating its 1,100 contact-centre agents from a keyword search tool to a Claude-based knowledge assistant. Training takes two hours per agent, and the agency cannot release more than 60 agents a week from the floor without breaching its published service level. The filing deadline is eighteen weeks away and the six weeks before it are peak, when call volume triples. The legacy search tool's support contract ends four weeks after the filing deadline and cannot be renewed. Which migration plan fits the constraints?

options.A: Raise the weekly release to 100 agents so all 1,100 are trained before peak begins, accepting a temporary service-level dip during the run-up.
options.B: Cut every agent over at week ten using a condensed one-hour session, so the whole floor is on a single tool throughout the peak period.
options.C: Train and migrate as many agents as the 60-a-week limit allows before peak, keep the legacy tool live for the remainder through the deadline, and finish the migration in the quiet weeks that follow.
options.D: Hold the entire migration until after the filing deadline so that no change of any kind lands near the busiest period of the year.

items.question: An energy retailer is holding the production readiness review for a Claude-based billing-query assistant. The reviewer already has the company's standard checklist covering capacity, backup and restore, on-call rotation and disaster recovery, all of which are closed. Which further items must be closed before sign-off because they exist only because this is an AI system? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: A load test demonstrating that the service sustains projected peak concurrency with the agreed headroom margin, repeated after every significant dependency change.
options.B: A rollback procedure for the prompt version and the pinned model version that does not require an application deployment.
options.C: A tested restore of the conversation store from backup completing inside the recovery time objective.
options.D: Named thresholds on output-quality proxies, each with an owner and a documented action when the threshold is breached.
options.E: A defined behaviour for what the assistant does, and what the customer sees, when a guardrail withholds an answer.

items.question: At 02:10 the run team for a retailer's Claude-based returns-authorisation assistant is paged: escalation-to-human rate has doubled. The dashboard shows the rate flat until 00:45 and climbing steadily since. No application deployment has happened for six days. The prompt registry records a new prompt version promoted at 00:40. A scheduled job re-indexed the knowledge base at 00:15, and the rate was unchanged between 00:15 and 00:45. The runbook documents a one-step revert for the prompt and a forty-minute rebuild to restore the previous index. What is the next step?

options.A: Revert the prompt to the previous version and re-check the escalation rate before touching the index.
options.B: Revert the prompt and rebuild the previous index at the same time, restoring the last fully known-good state as quickly as possible.
options.C: Wake the product team to read sample transcripts and identify the cause before making any change to the running configuration.
options.D: Raise the escalation-rate alert threshold to stop the paging overnight and investigate properly during business hours when the owners are available.

items.question: A platform team is retiring a shared Claude-based summarisation microservice used by nine downstream teams. Beyond the retirement date, what must the deprecation notice contain?

options.A: The reason for retirement and the saving it delivers to the platform budget, so consuming teams understand the rationale.
options.B: The replacement endpoint, a documented behavioural diff against the retiring service, and the date new integrations stop being accepted.
options.C: An invitation to object, with the retirement date reconsidered if enough consuming teams push back on the timeline.
options.D: The full changelog of the retiring service since its launch, so consuming teams can see how its behaviour evolved and judge how much of that behaviour they have come to depend on.

items.question: A logistics broker's Claude-based freight-quote assistant has an improvement backlog built entirely from sales-team feature requests. Its regression suite has held steady at 240 cases for four months, gaining nothing, while three production quality incidents occurred in the same period. The engineering manager asks what should change about how the backlog is constructed.

options.A: Replace the request-driven backlog with a purely metric-driven one derived from the quality dashboard, so prioritisation follows measurement rather than opinion.
options.B: Move backlog ownership from the sales team to engineering, so that reliability and technical debt receive fair weighting against new features.
options.C: Grow the regression suite to 500 cases by sampling more production traffic, raising coverage before the next incident occurs.
options.D: Make every production incident produce at least one regression case, and rank incident-derived work above feature requests in each iteration.

items.question: A pet insurer reviews its Claude-based claims-photo triage assistant monthly and wants to shorten the loop between a production failure and the iteration that fixes it. Today, problems reach the team as anecdotes weeks later with no way to reproduce them. Which mechanisms close that loop? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A weekly export of aggregate customer satisfaction scores delivered to the product manager.
options.B: A monthly all-hands session where adjusters describe problems they hit during the month.
options.C: A quarterly benchmark comparing the assistant against a competing vendor product on a standard task set.
options.D: A one-click "this was wrong" control in the adjuster's screen that captures the full request context and files the case into a triage queue.
options.E: A scheduled job that samples low-confidence and human-overridden decisions into a labelling queue for review.

items.question: A hospital trust is enabling 350 ward clerks on a Claude-based discharge-letter drafter, with one 45-minute session per clerk and no realistic prospect of a second. The pilot found that the two dominant causes of bad output were clerks pasting notes belonging to the wrong patient, and clerks accepting a draft without checking the medication list against the source. What should the 45 minutes prioritise?

options.A: A drill on the two observed failure modes: verifying patient identity before pasting, and a mandatory medication-list check worked through on a draft that got it wrong.
options.B: A structured overview of the assistant's capabilities and limitations, with time reserved for clerks to ask their own questions.
options.C: Prompt-writing technique, so clerks can steer drafts toward the trust's house style and reduce the editing burden on each letter.
options.D: The trust's AI governance policy and the clerk's personal accountability for anything they sign off under it.

items.question: How do pilot exit criteria differ in purpose from production readiness criteria?

options.A: Pilot exit criteria are qualitative judgements gathered from users, whereas readiness criteria are quantitative thresholds measured by instrumentation.
options.B: Pilot exit criteria are owned by the engineering team, whereas readiness criteria are owned by the business sponsor who funds the work.
options.C: Exit criteria test whether the value is real; readiness criteria test whether the organisation can run it.
options.D: Pilot exit criteria concern the model's behaviour, whereas readiness criteria concern the infrastructure the model is deployed onto.

items.question: A consultancy built a Claude-based grant-application scoring assistant for a philanthropic foundation and its engagement ends in thirty days. The foundation has two internal developers, neither of whom has worked on an LLM system before. Current state: the evaluation harness runs only from the consultancy's laptops via a local script; prompts are in a Git repository the foundation owns; the pinned model version is set by hand as an environment variable in the cloud console; the foundation's developers have already drafted a runbook from the design documents but have never run the evaluations or changed the model version themselves. With thirty days, what should the consultancy do first?

options.A: Write and hand over a formal runbook to consultancy standards, since a runbook drafted by people who have never operated the system cannot be relied on in an incident.
options.B: Deliver a two-week hands-on programme for the two developers covering LLM fundamentals and a walkthrough of the system's design decisions.
options.C: Negotiate a six-month support retainer so the foundation is never left without expertise, and complete the handover work gradually across that period.
options.D: Make the evaluation harness runnable in the foundation's own CI and move the pinned model version into the versioned configuration the prompts already use.

items.question: A telco is decommissioning a Claude-based network-fault summariser after eighteen months in service. Its outputs were attached to roughly 400,000 engineer work orders that the regulator may inspect for the next six years. The decommission plan already covers the standard steps. Which obligations does the sunset plan carry that a conventional application decommission would not? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Cancelling the service's cloud subscriptions and releasing its reserved accelerator capacity once the final batch of work orders has been archived.
options.B: Removing DNS records and load-balancer rules so that nothing in the estate continues to route toward the retired summariser endpoints.
options.C: Retaining, for each historical output, the prompt version, pinned model version and input context, so a past summary can be reconstructed if challenged.
options.D: Notifying the engineering population that the summariser is being withdrawn and confirming which manual step replaces it in the fault-handling workflow from cutover.
options.E: Preserving the record of which outputs an engineer amended and which were accepted unmodified, since accountability for a challenged summary turns on that.

items.question: In a production Claude system, what makes a prompt change a higher-risk deployment than a code change of comparable size?

options.A: Prompt changes cannot be meaningfully reviewed before merge, because their effect on output is not deterministic.
options.B: A prompt change can shift behaviour across every input class at once, and the effect is not visible from reading the diff.
options.C: Prompt changes bypass the application's automated test pipeline, because that pipeline exercises code paths and assertions rather than free text, and a prompt presents no code path to cover.
options.D: Prompt changes invalidate cached responses, producing a latency and cost spike immediately after deployment.

items.question: Eight weeks after launch, a building-materials distributor's Claude-based purchase-order query assistant is used weekly by 62% of its 400 target users, a figure flat for three weeks. The product owner proposes an internal marketing push. Session logs show that among the 152 non-users, 71% opened the assistant once and never returned, and their first sessions were disproportionately questions about a supplier catalogue the assistant has no connection to. What is the next step?

options.A: Connect the supplier catalogue to close the capability gap, then re-invite the roughly 108 users who tried the assistant once and left.
options.B: Run the internal marketing push as proposed, since awareness is the standard lever to reach for when weekly usage stops climbing at this stage.
options.C: Add a guided onboarding tutorial so that first sessions are more likely to end in a successful answer.
options.D: Survey the 152 non-users to establish why they are not returning before committing engineering effort.

items.question: A bank piloted a Claude-based small-business loan-document checker on 1,200 applications hand-picked by the pilot lead as representative, reaching 93% accuracy. Production intake includes 18% of applications submitted as phone-camera photographs of paper forms; the pilot set contained none, because the pilot lead excluded them as not a fair test. The lead also chose which applications to include in every other category. What should the architect insist on before production?

options.A: Proceed with the 93% figure and monitor accuracy closely in production, since photographed applications are a minority of intake and any problem will surface in the first weeks.
options.B: Proceed, adding a preprocessing step that diverts photographed applications into a manual queue so the checker only ever sees the kind of input it was measured on.
options.C: Re-measure on a random sample of real intake, photographs included, and set the production expectation from that number.
options.D: Run a second pilot on 1,200 photographed applications to obtain a segment-specific figure, then combine the two results weighted by volume share.

items.question: In an ownership transfer to a run team, what distinguishes the handover pack from the runbook?

options.A: The handover pack is authored by the build team, whereas the runbook is authored by the receiving run team once it has operated the system long enough to know what breaks.
options.B: The runbook holds procedures executed during an incident; the handover pack holds the context needed to make changes over the system's life.
options.C: The handover pack is a permanent record for audit, while the runbook is discarded once the run team is confident operating the system.
options.D: The runbook covers the application layer while the handover pack covers infrastructure, credentials and cloud accounts.

items.question: A grocery wholesaler's pilot of a Claude-based invoice-discrepancy assistant has ended and the steering group must decide on promotion to production. Which of the following, if true, constitute evidence that it should be promoted? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The accuracy threshold agreed before the pilot was met on a sample drawn randomly from real invoice intake.
options.B: Users rated the assistant highly in the post-pilot satisfaction survey, with most saying they would like to keep it.
options.C: The assistant's p95 latency sat comfortably inside the internal target throughout, measured on pilot traffic at a tenth of production volume.
options.D: The measured benefit exceeds the fully loaded run cost, including the human review time the workflow requires.
options.E: A named team has accepted operational ownership, with an on-call rotation and the authority to roll back.

items.question: A specialist translation agency introduced a Claude-based first-draft translator; its thirty senior linguists now post-edit rather than translate. Over four months, throughput rose 40%, three of the five most productive linguists resigned citing loss of craft, and the agency's independent quality audit score fell from 4.6 to 4.1 out of 5. The chief operating officer wants to accelerate the rollout to the remaining teams. What should the architect advise?

options.A: Pause the rollout and redesign the role so linguists retain original translation work on the content types where the audit score fell, before extending it further.
options.B: Accelerate as planned, since a 40% throughput gain is a larger and more durable commercial effect than a half-point movement on an internal five-point audit scale that customers never see.
options.C: Introduce a retention bonus for senior linguists, targeted at the individuals whose output the audit scores depend on most.
options.D: Move to a higher-capability model tier so first drafts require less post-editing, removing the repetitive work the linguists object to.

items.question: An internal platform team owns a Claude-based entity-extraction service used by four applications. A prompt change improves extraction recall but also changes date fields from free text to ISO-8601. Two of the four consumers parse dates with regular expressions tuned to the current format and will break. How should the change be shipped?

options.A: Ship to all four consumers with a release note; ISO-8601 is unambiguously the better format, and updating a regular expression is a small change each team can absorb inside a sprint.
options.B: Add a permanent compatibility layer that renders ISO dates back into the current free-text format, so no consumer ever has to change.
options.C: Version the endpoint and keep both versions running indefinitely, so each consumer migrates only if and when it chooses to.
options.D: Ship behind a per-consumer flag defaulting to current behaviour, with a dated cutover once both affected consumers confirm they have migrated.

items.question: During a routine review, the run team at a freight forwarder finds that the live system prompt in the configuration store differs from the version in the Git repository. The store's audit log shows an edit made three weeks ago from a developer's account, outside the deployment pipeline. Quality metrics have been stable throughout the three weeks, and the current live prompt has never been through the evaluation gate. What is the next step?

options.A: Capture the live prompt as a new versioned commit through the normal pipeline, then close the direct-write path so only the pipeline can change the store.
options.B: Revert the store to the repository version immediately, since the live prompt is unreviewed and source control must be the authority.
options.C: Open a disciplinary process against the developer whose account made the out-of-band change before altering anything in the environment.
options.D: Add a nightly reconciliation job that alerts the run team whenever the store and the repository diverge, and take the finding to the next iteration planning session for a decision.

items.question: What question should a post-implementation review answer that neither the pilot gate nor the production readiness review could?

options.A: Whether the system meets its latency and availability objectives at full production volume.
options.B: Whether the benefit forecast at the pilot gate actually materialised at scale, measured the way it was measured then.
options.C: Whether the architecture chosen was the best option available at the time the decision was taken, and what the team would choose if it were starting again today.
options.D: Whether the delivery team followed the organisation's project methodology and governance steps.

items.question: A payments firm's Claude-based sanctions-narrative assistant faces two competing demands. A regulator's thematic review requires that from 1 March, fourteen weeks away, every automated narrative cites the underlying rule applied. Separately, the operations team wants narratives shortened by 30%, which analysts estimate saves 900 analyst-hours a year. The team can absorb one substantial change per quarter. What should be scheduled first?

options.A: The length reduction, since 900 analyst-hours a year is a quantified recurring benefit and adding a rule citation is a formatting change that can be slotted in at short notice.
options.B: Neither yet; approach the supervisor for an extension so the team can sequence both changes against its own quality and release timeline.
options.C: The rule citation, because the date is externally set and missing it is a supervisory finding, while the length reduction carries no deadline.
options.D: Both in one release, since the citation lengthens narratives and the reduction offsets it, and a single release carries less change risk than two.

items.question: What does pinning a specific model version in a production system buy, and what obligation does it create?

options.A: It buys a lower and more predictable unit cost on inference, and obliges the team to renegotiate commercial terms at each contract renewal cycle.
options.B: It buys higher sustained throughput, and obliges the team to reserve capacity ahead of seasonal peaks.
options.C: It buys permanent immunity from provider-side behaviour changes, and creates no continuing obligation.
options.D: It buys reproducible behaviour across deployments, and obliges the team to plan and test a migration before that version retires.

items.question: A pharmacy-benefits manager is planning ring one of a Claude-based prior-authorisation assistant that will eventually cover 4,000 users across nine regions. The programme has agreed a quality threshold that ring one must clear before ring two opens. Which two properties should ring one have? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: It should consist entirely of volunteers, so that ring-one adoption rates predict adoption in the later rings.
options.B: It should include the region with the most atypical case mix, not only the most cooperative region.
options.C: It should be confined to a single region so the rollout can be described as geographically contained in board reporting.
options.D: It should exclude any region whose case mix differs from the national average, so that ring-one results are clean.
options.E: It should be large enough that the agreed quality threshold can actually be evaluated on the traffic it generates.

items.question: An airline moved passenger re-accommodation during irregular operations onto a Claude-based assistant eighteen months ago. During a recent 40-minute outage, the duty team's manual re-accommodation rate ran at about a third of the pre-automation rate, and two of the four duty managers had never performed the task without the assistant. The head of operations wants this addressed before the winter disruption season. What is the right response?

options.A: Schedule regular periods in which duty managers handle re-accommodation manually on live low-severity disruptions, and make demonstrated manual competence a condition of holding the duty rota.
options.B: Deploy the assistant across multiple regions to raise its availability, so outages become rare enough that the manual path effectively never has to carry load.
options.C: Document the manual procedure in full detail and require every duty manager to read and acknowledge it annually before the season starts.
options.D: Build a degraded mode in which a cheaper model tier serves re-accommodation decisions whenever the primary path is unavailable.

items.question: After training users to review the output of an AI assistant, which measurement best indicates that the enablement was effective?

options.A: The proportion of trained users who pass the end-of-session knowledge assessment.
options.B: The rate at which trained users correctly reject or amend incorrect output on seeded cases.
options.C: Weekly active usage among trained users compared against an untrained control group.
options.D: Self-reported confidence in reviewing assistant output, collected from users immediately after each session and again a month later.

items.question: A multinational manufacturer is rolling out a Claude-based safety-incident report assistant across 22 sites in six countries. It can phase by site — every incident type at one site, then the next — or by incident type — one type across all sites, then the next. The prompt and the retrieval index are built per incident type; site differences amount to interface language and a few local reporting fields, both handled through configuration. Which phasing should it choose?

options.A: Phase by site, so each phase sits inside a single management chain and the change can be led locally by that site's leadership.
options.B: Phase by region, grouping sites by time zone so that support coverage can follow the rollout around the clock.
options.C: Phase by incident type across all sites, so each phase validates one prompt-and-index artefact end to end.
options.D: Phase by incident type, but only at English-language sites first, deferring all localisation to a separate later programme.

items.question: A retailer's Claude-based gift-card fraud explanation feature is surfaced inside a third-party contact-centre platform the retailer does not control. The vendor releases quarterly and has refused to expose a feature flag. The retailer's production readiness review asks how a bad release would be withdrawn. What should the retailer require before go-live?

options.A: A contractual commitment from the vendor to ship an emergency release within 48 hours of a written request from the retailer.
options.B: Staged enablement by contact-centre team, configured through the vendor platform's existing user management features.
options.C: A pre-release soak in the vendor's staging environment covering a full quarter of historical traffic patterns before each release.
options.D: A kill switch in the retailer's own API that returns a defined unavailable response the vendor's interface already handles.

items.question: A regional water utility launched a Claude-based leak-report triage assistant ninety days ago and holds its first post-implementation review next week. Which items belong on the agenda because they answer questions neither the pilot gate nor the readiness review could? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: A retrospective assessment of whether a different architectural pattern would have suited the problem better.
options.B: The model provider's published roadmap for new capabilities the utility might adopt in the next financial year, and what each of them could be worth.
options.C: Whether the benefit forecast at the pilot gate has materialised at full volume, measured the same way it was measured at the gate.
options.D: The failure modes that appeared in production and were absent from the pilot, and what has entered the regression suite as a result.
options.E: Whether the operating model is working: who has been paged, how often, and whether the run team has acted without the build team.

items.question: A prompt change has caused a production quality regression. Under what condition is rolling forward with a corrected prompt preferable to reverting to the previous version?

options.A: When the previous version carries its own unresolved defect that the change was fixing, and the corrected prompt has passed the evaluation gate.
options.B: When the team is confident the fix is simple, since reverting a prompt always requires a full application release cycle and takes longer than shipping forward.
options.C: When the regression affects fewer users than the defect the original change was intended to fix.
options.D: When the prompt registry does not retain prior versions, leaving roll-forward as the only path available.

items.question: A media group's Claude-based archive-tagging service was built by a central innovation team on innovation funding. It is now in production serving three business units. At the first post-launch review, monthly spend is running at 3.4 times the pilot forecast, driven almost entirely by one unit's bulk re-tagging jobs. The innovation team's budget ends in two months and its engineers move to other work. Which two things must the lifecycle plan do? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Cap total monthly spend at the pilot forecast and throttle all requests once the cap is reached.
options.B: Extend the innovation team's funding for a further year while a chargeback model is designed and agreed.
options.C: Move the bulk re-tagging workload onto a cheaper model tier, chosen and applied by the central team before it disperses.
options.D: Attribute cost per business unit through request tagging and move run cost onto the consuming units' budgets, with the bulk re-tagging unit funding its own load.
options.E: Name a budget owner in each consuming unit who approves that unit's spend and receives its monthly consumption report.

items.question: Four weeks into an eight-week pilot of a Claude-based tender-response drafter at a construction firm, the sponsor emails: "Let's judge this on win rate rather than drafting hours saved." The criterion agreed before the pilot was a reduction in drafting hours. Tenders submitted during the pilot will not be decided for about five months, and the firm's own analyst says the pilot's forty tenders cannot distinguish a five-point change in win rate from noise. What is the next step?

options.A: Adopt win rate as the criterion, since it sits far closer to the commercial outcome the firm ultimately cares about than an activity measure such as drafting hours ever could.
options.B: Report both measures at the readout and let the sponsor decide how to weight them when the decision is taken.
options.C: Hold the agreed criterion for the pilot decision, and separately commit to a win-rate read at five months with a stated sample size requirement.
options.D: Extend the pilot until enough tenders have been submitted and decided to measure win rate directly.

items.question: Ninety days after launch, an AI feature's weekly active usage is high and still rising. Why is that insufficient as a measure of post-launch success?

options.A: Usage counts are typically inflated by automated health checks and synthetic monitoring traffic hitting the same endpoints.
options.B: Usage shows that people are engaging with the feature, not that the engagement produced the outcome the work was funded to deliver.
options.C: Usage cannot be compared across teams, because every team defines an active user slightly differently.
options.D: Usage is a lagging indicator, so by the time it moves in either direction the opportunity to intervene on the underlying cause has already passed.

items.question: A specialist lender piloted a Claude-based covenant-breach detector with two credit analysts reviewing every flagged case. The pilot covered 150 loans a week, flagged 11% of them, and each review took about 25 minutes. Production volume is 4,000 loans a week. The credit team has nine analysts with roughly 12 free hours each per week, headcount is frozen for the financial year, and the lender's credit policy requires every potential breach to be recorded and dispositioned. What does the production plan need?

options.A: Recruit the additional analyst capacity required to review every flagged case at production volume, and treat it as a running cost of the programme rather than a reason to redesign the control.
options.B: Raise the detection threshold until the number of flags fits comfortably inside the review hours the team already has available.
options.C: Reserve full review for a defined high-risk subset sized against the 108 available hours, with the remainder taking a lighter documented check.
options.D: Proceed with full review of every flag and manage the resulting queue, using queue age as the operational control and escalation trigger.

items.question: What is the purpose of running a scheduled drill of an AI system's runbook before ownership transfers to a run team?

options.A: To satisfy the assurance requirement that operational documentation exists and has been formally reviewed and signed.
options.B: To benchmark the model's latency under load so that capacity planning can be finalised before go-live.
options.C: To give the receiving team exposure to the system's architecture and design rationale in a low-pressure setting.
options.D: To find the steps that do not work: missing access, stale commands, approvals nobody can grant out of hours.

items.question: A Nordic bank is transferring its Claude-based transaction-narrative service to a run team seven hours ahead, in a different legal entity. The two teams overlap for about two working hours a day. The build team will remain available for three months, then disband. Which two adjustments to the standard handover most directly address the time-zone and entity split? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Grant the run team's entity its own credentials and rollback approval rights, so no production action requires an approver who is asleep or in another company.
options.B: Extend the build team's availability from three months to twelve, so that the two-hour overlap constraint matters less during the transition and the run team can take its time.
options.C: Move the daily handover session into the two-hour overlap and use it for a live incident replay driven by the run team, not for status reporting.
options.D: Record video walkthroughs of every runbook procedure so the run team can watch them outside the overlap window.
options.E: Route all production alerts to both teams for the full three months so nothing can be missed while the run team builds confidence.

items.question: Why must the evaluation suite transfer to the run team along with a production Claude system?

options.A: Without it the run team cannot tell whether a change or a fix is safe to deploy, so every subsequent change becomes a guess.
options.B: Evaluation results are required evidence for the organisation's annual audit of automated decision systems.
options.C: The evaluation suite is in practice the only place where the system's functional requirements have been written down in a form that can actually be executed and checked.
options.D: A model version cannot be pinned or migrated without an evaluation record accompanying the configuration.

items.question: Six months after launch, a wholesaler's Claude-based order-entry assistant shows 88% adoption and all quality metrics inside target, yet the forecast saving of 6 minutes per order has materialised as 1.4 minutes. A time-and-motion study finds the assistant does save 6 minutes on drafting, but staff now spend 4.6 minutes reconciling its output into the ERP by hand because the assistant cannot write to it. The study attributes that time to manual re-keying, not to correcting errors. What should the team do?

options.A: Report the realised 1.4-minute saving, revise the business case downward, and record the programme as delivering a smaller but genuine benefit.
options.B: Invest in raising the assistant's accuracy so that staff have less to reconcile when they transfer output into the ERP.
options.C: Prioritise the ERP write integration, since that is where the forecast benefit is being consumed, and re-read the benefit once it ships.
options.D: Retire the assistant, because a 1.4-minute saving per order does not justify the ongoing run cost and the change management overhead.

items.question: Why do user-reported issues systematically understate an AI system's production failure rate?

options.A: Because the system logs its own failures separately from the user reporting channel, and the two counts are never reconciled.
options.B: Because users cannot report a failure they did not notice, and confidently wrong output is precisely the failure that does not announce itself.
options.C: Because most production failures occur outside core hours, when fewer users are active to observe them.
options.D: Because users who are unsure about an output tend to file a report anyway, which inflates rather than deflates the recorded count and buries the genuine failures among them.

items.question: An insurer acquires a competitor. Both operate a Claude-based first-notice-of-loss triage assistant. The acquirer's handles 9,000 claims a month and has a documented evaluation suite, a pinned model version and a named run team. The acquired one handles 3,500 a month, has no evaluation suite, and is tightly coupled to the acquired company's policy administration system, whose own migration is a separate programme expected to take at least three years. The integration lead proposes retiring the acquired assistant immediately. What should the architect advise?

options.A: Retire the acquired assistant now and route its 3,500 claims a month to the acquirer's assistant, funding the necessary policy-system integration work as a one-off cost of the merger.
options.B: Keep both systems permanently, since each is coupled to a different policy administration platform and neither dependency is going away soon.
options.C: Build a single new assistant that serves both policy systems and retire both existing ones once it reaches parity with each.
options.D: Bring the acquired assistant under the acquirer's operating model — evaluation suite, pinned version, run-team ownership — and tie its sunset date to the policy-system migration.
